If we take the steam engine example, once a patent is published, everyone in the world can see that invention. Maybe the inventor was on to something, or maybe after everyone can look at the specification, it's clearly an inefficient design and someone else can come up with a better way of making a steam engine.

Let's say he was on to something (scenario 1). Someone else can come up with an improvement to it, and everyone is theoretically incentivized to make a deal - the original inventor has a monopoly in his original steam engine, but he REALLY wants to sell engines with the new improvement, and the second inventor can't sell his invention without the rights to the original engine. However, even if no deal is made, improvements are constantly being given to the world because all these patents are published. In 20 years, everyone can use everything - so who comes out on top after 20 years? The original inventor who wouldn't make a deal with anyone, or a savvy business inventor who chooses to license his steam engine design to people for an appropriate amount of money?

Let's say he wasn't on to anything in the first place (scenario 2). People can see the areas where he succeeded/failed, and maybe avoid those in the future. With a perfect patent system (I grant you that we don't have one), we don't have people trying the same failed design over and over because they'll be able to see the failures and see which direction is correct. Further, maybe the idea that the original inventor had was good, but his patented invention is actually pretty bad. Other people can see that and create a better steam engine that isn't covered by his patent.

Without a patent system, everything moves towards Trade Secrets. Without patents, no one will tell you how anything works - you've got to reverse engineer it, if you can get your hands on it in the first place. Perhaps that's possible with a steam engine, barring any sort of contractual obligations / hired guards / whatever other protections someone tries to protect an engine with, but it might be a lot harder with software. Some things are vastly more valuable as trade secrets - think of the Coke recipe, or the KFC recipe. If we could have had duplicate Coke 20 years after Coke first came out, wouldn't that be better than infinitely paying Coke money? It would force Coke to innovate, not rely on its old products, or make them focus on added value to their products.

Our system is more broken then it is working. Patent trolls is a big problem we haven't even touched on yet. Where patents are used to extract protection money from others who unknowingly "discovered/invented" the same thing. I fully agree that it would be more secure if there were an option to not do it at all for those who either did not need to use more than one client, or who were sophisticated enough to do their own secure key distribution of their private key among their devices (and some will be - a lot of folks who would be interested in this have probably used a pgp keyring at one point or another). I am also a bit leery of the amount of original crypto implementation that this project entails. There's a lot of peer review and poking and prodding to be done here, but that'll be necessary for any much-needed advancements toward the goal of encrypting as much of our normal infrastructure as we can.

That said, if one accepts that a mechanism to allow users to distribute their private key among multiple clients should be provided, and assuming I understand what they're doing correctly, I think they picked a good approach, which was to allow a user to create a secret symmetric key (the hash of their chosen password) which never leaves any client and use that to encrypt the RSA private key which is then distributed in encrypted form. Single points of failure whose key strength are computable are okay in encryption systems, it's additional points of failure that are the concern. This qualifies as that, so I agree with your point. I believe they wrestled with it as a design decision, as evidenced by the mention of a password strength validator in the client. I haven't looked at it.
